imgs.a: Rough endoplasmic reticulum on electron microscopy

qs.q: An electron microscopy study of a cultured fibroblast focuses on the structural network providing mechanical support and intracellular transport. Which components constitute the primary elements of the cellular cytoskeleton?
o: Actin networks, nuclear lamina, and the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Endoplasmic reticulum, microtubules, and intermediate filaments
qs.e: The cytoskeleton is composed of microtubules, intermediate filaments, and microfilaments, which together maintain cell shape and motility. The endoplasmic reticulum is an intracellular membrane system, not a cytoskeletal element.

qs.q: Which component of the cytoskeleton is the largest and provides the basis for complex cytoplasmic structures like cilia and flagella?
qs.e: Microtubules are the largest cytoskeletal components, composed of globular protein subunits, and provide the basis for structures like cilia, flagella, and mitotic structures. Microfilaments are the smallest and are composed of actin.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome. Which best explains why this mutation leads to disease? Dystrophin anchors the cytoskeleton to the membrane; without it, muscle fibers tear during contraction. ---
o: Impaired immune surveillance against abnormal muscle fibers
Defective structural protein disrupting muscle cell membrane stability
Loss of DNA repair capacity leading to increased mutations
Defective enzyme causing substrate accumulation in lysosomes
Failure of apoptosis leading to accumulation of abnormal myocytes
qs.e: Dystrophin is a structural protein that anchors the cytoskeleton, and its absence destabilizes the muscle cell membrane.

ai.title: Cytoskeleton
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The cytoskeleton is the cell’s structural framework, essential for shape, transport and division. In disease, mutations or infections disrupt its components, leading to hemolysis, muscular dystrophy or impaired cell migration.

sections.p: The cytoskeleton consists of actin microfilaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments, linked by adaptor proteins. Diagnosis is usually indirect, via clinical syndromes and genetic testing.

t.b: Shows abnormal red cell shapes (e.g., elliptocytes, spherocytes) indicating cytoskeletal defects

t.a: Genetic panel for spectrin, ankyrin, dystrophin
t.b: Confirms hereditary hemolytic anemias or muscular dystrophies
Reveals structural abnormalities in dystrophin or desmin

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical impact: mild hemolysis, moderate anemia, or severe muscle weakness. Staging follows established scales: e.g., the 5‑point scale for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) based on functional milestones.
b: Moderate: noticeable anemia or muscle cramps

t.b: Defines anemia severity; <30% indicates moderate to severe
Predicts respiratory compromise in DMD; <50% predicted is severe

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections and nutritional deficiencies can precipitate cytoskeletal dysfunction. Genetic causes remain the primary etiology.
b: Sickle cell disease (HbS polymerisation affecting actin)

t.b: Detects HbS, HbC, HbE common in Africa

sections.p: Patients may have chronic anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, or progressive muscle weakness. Acute crises can mimic sepsis or heart failure.
b: Muscle cramps, waddling gait, respiratory distress

t.b: Look for splenomegaly, calf pseudohypertrophy, or calf pseudohypertrophy

sections.p: Tests are chosen to confirm the underlying defect and assess severity. In resource‑poor settings, focus on inexpensive, high‑yield tests.

t.b: Identifies abnormal RBC morphology; elliptocytes suggest spectrin defects
Elevated in hemolytic anemia; normal in aplastic crises

sections.p: Complications include severe anemia, heart failure, respiratory failure, and infections due to splenectomy or immunosuppression.

t.b: Watch for tachycardia, hypotension, or worsening dyspnea

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor organ function. Drug choices consider availability and safety.
b: Hydroxyurea in sickle cell to reduce crises
Avoid NSAIDs in DMD due to renal risk

t.b: Reduces hemolysis and improves oxygen delivery
Maintains muscle strength and joint mobility

sections.p: Regular monitoring of hemoglobin, growth, and respiratory function is essential. Preventive measures include malaria prophylaxis and vaccination.
Other hemolytic anemias and muscular disorders share overlapping features.
b: Hereditary spherocytosis vs. autoimmune hemolytic anemia

t.b: Positive in autoimmune hemolysis, negative in hereditary forms

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal in early disease or due to concurrent infections.
b: Haptoglobin may be normal in extravascular hemolysis
Reticulocyte count can be low if marrow is suppressed by infection

faq.q: What is the most common cytoskeletal protein defect in Africa?
faq.a: Spectrin or ankyrin mutations causing hereditary spherocytosis.
Yes, malaria parasites can damage RBC membranes, exacerbating hemolysis.

faq.q: Why avoid NSAIDs in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
faq.a: They increase renal risk and worsen muscle breakdown.

exam: A 10‑year‑old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and calf pseudohypertrophy. What is the next best diagnostic step? — Genetic testing for dystrophin deletion; consider muscle biopsy if unavailable.
A patient with chronic hemolytic anemia has a normal haptoglobin level but high bilirubin. What explains this? — Extravascular hemolysis; haptoglobin is consumed in intravascular hemolysis.
During a malaria outbreak, a patient with known hereditary spherocytosis develops sudden jaundice. What is the most likely cause? — Malaria‑induced hemolysis superimposed on underlying defect.
A 7‑year‑old with anemia has a peripheral smear showing elliptocytes. Which gene is most likely mutated? — Protein 4.1 or glycophorin C.
A patient with DMD is started on NSAIDs for pain. What complication should you monitor? — Renal dysfunction and worsening muscle breakdown.
A child with splenomegaly and anemia is found to have a positive direct antiglobulin test. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not hereditary spherocytosis.
A patient with chronic hemolysis is scheduled for elective surgery. What pre‑operative test is essential? — Baseline hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and haptoglobin to assess ongoing hemolysis.
